South Dakota.ag_notification_note: The company must tell the Attorney General only if the breach affects more than 250 South Dakota residents. It must also tell the nationwide credit bureaus whenever it notifies residents.
South Dakota.freeze_rights_note: You can place a free security freeze on your credit file at Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion — federal law makes freezes free, and you must place one separately at each bureau. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name until you lift it.
South Dakota.notification_deadline_note: The company must tell you no later than 60 days after it discovers the breach or is told about it. Notice can be delayed if law enforcement needs it held back, and then it must go out within 30 days after law enforcement says it is okay. No notice is owed at all if the company investigates, tells the Attorney General, and reasonably finds the breach is not likely to harm you.
South Dakota.private_right_note: You cannot sue under this law yourself. Only the Attorney General can enforce it, as a deceptive act, with civil penalties of up to $10,000 per day per violation.
South Dakota.state_note: South Dakota is one of the few states with a harm test: if the company investigates and reasonably decides the breach will not likely harm you, it can skip telling you — but it still has to tell the Attorney General and keep its written reasoning for three years.

Tennessee.ag_notification_note: Tennessee law does not require the company to notify the Attorney General at all. If more than 1,000 people are notified at once, the company must tell the nationwide credit bureaus instead.
Tennessee.freeze_rights_note: You can place a free security freeze on your credit file at Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion — federal law makes freezes free, and you must place one separately at each bureau. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name until you lift it.
Tennessee.legal_aid_name: Legal Aid Society of Middle Tennessee and the Cumberlands
Tennessee.notification_deadline_note: The company must tell you no later than 45 days after it discovers the breach or is told about it. Notice can be delayed if law enforcement says it would impede a criminal investigation, and then it must go out within 45 days after law enforcement clears it.
Tennessee.private_right_note: Yes. Under Tenn. Code Ann. § 47-18-2107(h), any injured customer (other than a state agency) may sue the company for damages and ask a court to order it to stop violating the law.
Tennessee.state_note: Tennessee is unusual in two ways: the company never has to tell the Attorney General, but you can sue the company directly for damages if it breaks this law — most states give you no such right.

Texas.ag_notification_note: The company must notify the Attorney General only if the breach involves at least 250 Texas residents. Since September 1, 2023 (SB 768), that AG notice is due as soon as practicable and within 30 days — faster than the 60-day deadline for telling you — and must be filed electronically through the AG's website.
Texas.freeze_rights_note: You can place a free security freeze on your credit file at Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion — federal law makes freezes free, and you must place one separately at each bureau. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name until you lift it.
Texas.notification_deadline_note: The company must tell you without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 days after the date it determines the breach occurred. It may take extra time to figure out the scope of the breach and fix its systems, or if law enforcement asks for a delay.
Texas.private_right_note: You cannot sue under this law yourself. Only the Attorney General enforces it, with civil penalties of $2,000 to $50,000 per violation plus up to $100 per person per day for failing to notify (capped at $250,000 per breach).
Texas.state_note: Texas posts breach reports publicly: the Attorney General must publish a listing of the breach notifications it receives on its website, so you can check whether a breach affecting you was reported.
Texas.statute_name: Identity Theft Enforcement and Protection Act

Utah.ag_notification_note: The company must notify the Office of the Attorney General and the Utah Cyber Center only if the breach involves misuse affecting 500 or more Utah residents. If 1,000 or more residents are affected, it must also tell the nationwide credit bureaus.
Utah.freeze_rights_note: You can place a free security freeze on your credit file at Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion — federal law makes freezes free, and you must place one separately at each bureau. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name until you lift it.
Utah.notification_deadline_note: Utah sets no fixed number of days. Once the company's investigation finds that misuse of your information has happened or is reasonably likely, it must tell you in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay, allowing time to determine the scope of the breach and restore its systems.
Utah.private_right_note: No. Utah Code § 13-44-301 expressly says the law creates no private right of action. Only the Attorney General enforces it, with penalties up to $2,500 per consumer and $100,000 in total — though claims you already have under other laws, like contract or tort, are preserved.
Utah.state_note: Utah has a harm test: the company must first investigate in good faith, and it only has to notify you if that investigation finds misuse has happened or is reasonably likely — a breach alone, with no likely misuse, triggers no notice to you.

Vermont.ag_notification_note: Yes, for every breach. The company must give the Attorney General (or the Department of Financial Regulation, for businesses that agency regulates) a preliminary notice within 14 business days of discovery or of notifying consumers, whichever comes first, and must send the AG a copy of the consumer notice.
Vermont.freeze_rights_note: You can place a free security freeze on your credit file at Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion — federal law makes freezes free, and you must place one separately at each bureau. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name until you lift it. Vermont's own freeze law also makes freezes free.
Vermont.notification_deadline_note: The company must tell you in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay, but no later than 45 days after it discovers the breach or is told about it. Notice can be delayed at law enforcement's request while an investigation is underway.
Vermont.private_right_note: No. The Attorney General and the State's Attorney have sole authority to investigate and enforce the law. A violation is treated as a Consumer Protection Act violation, with penalties up to $10,000 per violation.
Vermont.state_note: Vermont has the fastest regulator clock in this group: the company must give the Attorney General a preliminary heads-up within 14 business days, well before the 45-day deadline for telling you — and the AG posts consumer breach notices on its website.

Virginia.ag_notification_note: Yes, for every breach — the Attorney General must be told whenever any Virginia resident is notified, with no minimum number of people. If more than 1,000 people are notified at once, the company must also tell the nationwide credit bureaus.
Virginia.freeze_rights_note: You can place a free security freeze on your credit file at Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion — federal law makes freezes free, and you must place one separately at each bureau. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name until you lift it.
Virginia.notification_deadline_note: Virginia sets no fixed number of days. The company must tell you and the Attorney General without unreasonable delay after discovering the breach. It may take reasonable time to determine the scope and fix its systems, or delay if law enforcement says notice would impede an investigation.
Virginia.private_right_note: Limited. There is no general right to sue under this law, but the statute preserves your ability to recover direct economic damages caused by a violation. The Attorney General enforces the law and can impose a civil penalty up to $150,000 per breach.
Virginia.state_note: Virginia's law sits in the criminal code, not the business code, and its definition of personal information is broader than most: passport numbers and military identification numbers count, along with Social Security and driver's license numbers.

Washington.ag_notification_note: The company must notify the Attorney General only if the breach affects more than 500 Washington residents in a single breach, and that notice is also due within 30 days of discovery. State agencies get up to 14 extra days to translate notices.
Washington.freeze_rights_note: You can place a free security freeze on your credit file at Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion — federal law makes freezes free, and you must place one separately at each bureau. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name until you lift it.
Washington.notification_deadline_note: The company must tell you in the most expedient time possible and within 30 days after the breach was discovered — one of the strictest deadlines in the country. It can only delay for law enforcement needs or for the time needed to determine the scope of the breach and restore its systems. No notice is required if the breach is not reasonably likely to put you at risk of harm.
Washington.private_right_note: Yes. Under RCW 19.255.040, any consumer injured by a violation may sue for damages, and a violator may also be enjoined. The Attorney General may sue on behalf of the state as well, but AG actions under this chapter cannot be brought under the Consumer Protection Act's private-suit provision.
Washington.state_note: Washington is the strictest state in this group: a 30-day deadline, plain-language notices that must say what data was taken, AG notice at 500 people, and a direct right for you to sue for damages — plus a separate breach law (RCW 42.56.590) that covers state and local agencies.
Washington.statute_name: Personal Information — Notice of Security Breaches

West Virginia.ag_notification_note: West Virginia law requires no notice to the Attorney General. If more than 1,000 people are notified at once, the company must tell the nationwide credit bureaus instead.
West Virginia.freeze_rights_note: You can place a free security freeze on your credit file at Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion — federal law makes freezes free, and you must place one separately at each bureau. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name until you lift it.
West Virginia.notification_deadline_note: West Virginia sets no fixed number of days. The company must tell you without unreasonable delay after discovering the breach, allowing time to determine the scope and restore its systems, or if law enforcement asks for a delay. Notice is only owed if unencrypted, unredacted information was taken and identity theft or fraud has happened or is likely.
West Virginia.private_right_note: No. Only the Attorney General enforces the law, and civil penalties apply only for repeated and willful violations, capped at $150,000 per breach or series of breaches.
West Virginia.state_note: West Virginia is light on deadlines and regulator notice: no fixed day count, no AG notice, and no notice at all unless the stolen data was unencrypted and identity theft or fraud is caused or likely — but the breach letter itself must tell you about fraud alerts and security freezes.
West Virginia.statute_name: Breach of Security of Consumer Information

Wisconsin.ag_notification_note: Wisconsin law requires no notice to the Attorney General or any regulator. If 1,000 or more people must be notified in a single incident, the company must tell the nationwide credit bureaus instead.
Wisconsin.freeze_rights_note: You can place a free security freeze on your credit file at Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion — federal law makes freezes free, and you must place one separately at each bureau. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name until you lift it. Wisconsin's consumer protection agency for identity theft complaints is the Department of Agriculture, Trade and Consumer Protection (DATCP).
Wisconsin.notification_deadline_note: The company must tell you within a reasonable time, and no later than 45 days after it learns your personal information was acquired. What counts as reasonable takes into account how many notices it must send and how it can reach people. Law enforcement can ask the company to hold notice to protect an investigation.
Wisconsin.private_right_note: No. The statute creates no private right of action (Fox v. Iowa Health System). Failing to notify you is not negligence by itself, but it can be used as evidence of negligence in a lawsuit under other law. The Attorney General enforces the law.
Wisconsin.state_note: Wisconsin's notice duty has a no-risk escape hatch: no notice is owed if the acquisition creates no material risk of identity theft or fraud — and if you do get a notice, you can write to the company and demand it tell you exactly which of your information was acquired.
Wisconsin.statute_name: Notice of Unauthorized Acquisition of Personal Information

Wyoming.ag_notification_note: Wyoming law requires no notice to the Attorney General or any other regulator. There is no regulator-notice provision in the statute at all.
Wyoming.freeze_rights_note: You can place a free security freeze on your credit file at Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion — federal law makes freezes free, and you must place one separately at each bureau. A freeze blocks new accounts from being opened in your name until you lift it.
Wyoming.notification_deadline_note: Wyoming sets no fixed number of days. After the company investigates and finds that misuse of your information has happened or is reasonably likely, it must tell you as soon as possible, in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay, allowing for law enforcement needs and for scoping the breach and restoring its systems.
Wyoming.private_right_note: No. Only the Attorney General may bring an action to enforce the law and recover damages or other relief. You cannot sue under this statute yourself.
Wyoming.state_note: Wyoming is one of the most consumer-unfriendly setups in this group for timing: no day count, no regulator notice, and the company only has to tell you after its own investigation concludes misuse happened or is likely — so if you hear about a breach secondhand, ask the company directly what it found.
Wyoming.statute_name: Computer Security Breach; Notice to Affected Persons
